a3330.speech: Affirmed its firm position and decisions regarding terrorism and extremism regardless of its source, its rejection of all forms and manifestations, its work to eliminate sources of financing and its support for international efforts to combat terrorism, and that terrorism is not associated with any religion, culture, nationality or ethnic group; condemned all terrorist acts, stressed the sanctity of bloodshed and of attacks on civilians and civilian facilities such as schools, places of worship and hospitals, and stressed the importance of international and regional coordination against terrorist groups and sectarian militias ; stressed the importance of strengthening the values of dialogue and respect between peoples and cultures and condemned offensive statements against Islam, Muslims and Islamic civilization ; called for deterrent measures to combat terrorism, extremism, hate speech and incitement in accordance with Security Council resolutions 2686 (2023) and 2734 (2024) ; condemned the continued external support for terrorist groups and sectarian armed formations in the Middle East.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Condemned a series of specific attacks: the terrorist attack on a Pakistani army post in the Makin area of Waziristan on 21 December 2024 which killed 16 soldiers; the terrorist ramming incidents in the Federal Republic of Germany on 20 December 2024 and 13 February 2025; the hit-and-run incident in New Orleans and the explosion in front of a hotel in Las Vegas, USA, on 1 January 2025; the shooting in Cetinje, Montenegro, on 2 January 2025; the terrorist attack on the presidential palace in N'Djamena, Chad, on 9 January 2025; the terrorist attack on army forces in the Alibori region of Benin on 12 January 2025; and the shooting in Orebro, Sweden, on 5 February 2025 - expressing condolences and solidarity with the victims, their families and the governments and peoples concerned.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Affirmed its firm position and decisions regarding relations with Iran, stressing the need for Iran to adhere to the Charter of the United Nations, the principles of good neighbourliness, respect for the sovereignty of states, non-interference in internal affairs, the settlement of disputes by peaceful means and the rejection of the use or threat of force, terrorism, extremism and sectarianism ; expressed concern over developments in the Iranian nuclear file, stressing the importance of accelerating a constructive understanding and the readiness of the GCC countries to participate in all related negotiations, which must include, in addition to the nuclear programme, ballistic and cruise missiles and drones and the security of international navigation and oil facilities ; stressed the importance of Iran's commitments not to exceed uranium enrichment levels necessary for peaceful use and to cooperate fully with the International Atomic Energy Agency ; stressed the importance of maintaining maritime security and waterways in the region.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Affirmed its full support for the Presidential Leadership Council in Yemen headed by Dr. Rashad Mohammed Al-Alimi and for reaching a comprehensive political solution in accordance with the Gulf Initiative, the outcomes of the Comprehensive National Dialogue Conference and Security Council Resolution 2216 ; welcomed the efforts of Saudi Arabia and Oman and renewed its support for the UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg ; called on the Yemeni parties to fully implement the commitments announced to the UN envoy on 23 December 2023, including a comprehensive nationwide ceasefire ; expressed deep concern over developments in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, condemning foreign interference in Yemen's internal affairs and the smuggling of military experts and weapons to the Houthi militias in violation of Security Council resolutions 2216, 2231 and 2624 ; appreciated Oman's role in releasing the detained crew of the ship (Galaxy) and called on the Houthis to immediately release all detained staff working for the UN, the US Embassy, international organisations and other diplomatic missions.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Highly appreciated the new economic support provided by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to Yemen, amounting to 500 million US dollars, including a 300 million dollar deposit in the Central Bank of Yemen and 200 million dollars to support the closing of Yemen's budget deficit, out of a total of 1.2 billion dollars through the Saudi Program for the Development and Reconstruction of Yemen ; welcomed the bilateral financial arrangements agreement signed by the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development and the Republic of Yemen ; welcomed the outcomes of the 22nd meeting of the Joint Technical Committee for Identifying the Development Needs of the Republic of Yemen ; praised the achievements of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center and the humanitarian and development assistance provided by all the GCC countries to Yemen, noting 263 development projects and initiatives in 7 basic sectors and the Saudi Mine Action Project (MASAM), which removed 480,526 mines, unexploded ordnance and explosive devices and cleared 64,691,637 square metres of land in Yemen.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Affirmed its firm position and decisions regarding the brotherly Republic of Iraq and its support for ongoing efforts to achieve security and stability there, stressing the importance of preserving Iraq's territorial integrity, full sovereignty, Arab identity, social fabric and national unity, and condemning all terrorist operations against Iraq ; highly appreciated the positive partnership between the Cooperation Council and Iraq and stressed the need to complete the electricity interconnection project ; welcomed the resumption of the Kuwaiti-Iraqi Joint Technical and Legal Committee on the demarcation of the maritime boundary beyond Marker 162 and stressed the importance of Iraq's respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the State of Kuwait, its compliance with Security Council Resolution 833 (1993) and with the Khor Abdullah navigation agreement, expressing complete rejection of the reasoning of the Iraqi Federal Supreme Court's decision and considering any unilateral Iraqi decisions on Khor Abdullah null and void ; stressed its support for Security Council Resolution 2732 (2024) and for continued Security Council monitoring of the file of Kuwaiti prisoners, missing persons and property, and said that the fair and most appropriate alternative after the end of UNAMI is the appointment of a high-level representative of the Secretary-General.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Stressed the importance of respecting the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the brotherly Syrian Arab Republic and of rejecting foreign interference in its internal affairs ; congratulated President Ahmed al-Sharaa on assuming the presidency of the Syrian Arab Republic during the transitional stage ; welcomed the content of his speech of 30 January 2025 and the convening of the Syrian National Dialogue Conference on 25 February 2025 ; welcomed the outcomes of the International Ministerial Conference on Syria held in Paris on 13 February 2025 and of the Riyadh meetings statement of 12 January 2025 ; called on all parties and components of the Syrian people to unite their efforts, integrate armed groups under the Ministry of Defence and restrict the bearing of weapons to the state ; condemned all acts of violence aimed at destabilising Syria and Israel's repeated attacks on Syria, including the occupation of the buffer zone, stressing that the Golan Heights are Syrian Arab land ; called for the lifting of sanctions on the Syrian Arab Republic and welcomed the positive steps taken by the United States, the European Union and the United Kingdom to ease some of the sanctions imposed on Syria ; noted the generous assistance and humanitarian air bridges provided by the GCC countries to the brotherly Syrian people.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Affirmed the GCC's firm position towards the brotherly Lebanese Republic and its unwavering support for Lebanon's sovereignty, security and stability, stressing the importance of comprehensive structural political and economic reforms ; congratulated President Joseph Aoun on his election victory and welcomed the content of his inaugural speech of 9 January 2025, the outcomes of his visit to Saudi Arabia on 3 March 2025 and the formation of a new government headed by Nawaf Salam ; stressed the need to adhere to the ceasefire agreement in Lebanon, condemning the continuation of Israeli attacks which have led to thousands of civilian casualties ; condemned the attack on UNIFIL ; highly appreciated the UAE's decision to reopen its embassy in Lebanon ; stressed the need to implement Security Council resolutions on Lebanon, especially Resolution 1701, and the Taif Agreement ; affirmed its support for the efforts of the Quintet on Lebanon ; called for the intensification of international and regional efforts to provide urgent humanitarian support to Lebanon and noted the assistance provided by the GCC countries to the brotherly Lebanese people.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Stressed the GCC's firm position on the importance of preserving the sovereignty, security, stability and territorial integrity of Sudan, of promoting dialogue and returning to the path of a political process leading to civilian rule, and called on the Sudanese parties to participate seriously in initiatives to settle the crisis, including the Jeddah forum ; stressed the importance of the two parties' commitment to the Jeddah Declaration of 11 May 2023 and the declaration of 20 May 2023 ; condemned the attack on the Saudi hospital in El Fasher on 26 January 2025 ; expressed concern over the humanitarian crisis in the Republic of Sudan, stressing Security Council Resolution 2417 (2018) and affirming Resolution 2736 of 13 June 2024 calling for an immediate ceasefire and the full, rapid, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid ; highly appreciated the humanitarian assistance and air bridges provided by the GCC countries to the brotherly Sudanese people.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Stressed the importance of restoring security and stability in the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, of non-discrimination in education and work, of protecting minorities, and of ensuring that Afghan lands are not used by terrorist groups or exploited for narcotics ; affirmed the GCC's solidarity with the people of Afghanistan in combating terrorism ; condemned the explosion at the Ministry of Refugees in Kabul on 11 December 2024 which killed the Minister of Refugees and Repatriation of the interim government, and the terrorist explosion in Kunduz province on 11 February 2025 and the terrorist act in Kabul on 13 February 2025.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Stressed that the GCC's position on the Russian-Ukrainian crisis is based on the principles of international law and the UN Charter, on preserving the international system based on respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of states, on non-interference in internal affairs and on the non-use or threat of force ; highly appreciated the diplomatic efforts of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its hosting of negotiations between the Russian Federation and the United States of America on the Ukrainian crisis in Riyadh on 18 February 2025 ; affirmed its support for the mediation efforts of the GCC countries and highly appreciated the success of the UAE's mediation, which led to an exchange involving 2,883 prisoners from both sides and the return of Russian children to their families ; noted the humanitarian aid provided to Ukraine by the GCC countries and stressed the importance of continuing to support efforts to facilitate the export of grain and foodstuffs.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Welcomed the outcomes of the joint ministerial meetings held on 6 March 2025 in Makkah Al-Mukarramah between the Cooperation Council and, respectively, the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan (with Ayman Safadi), the Arab Republic of Egypt (with Badr Abdelatty), the Kingdom of Morocco (with Nasser Bourita) and the Syrian Arab Republic (with Asaad Al-Shaibani), stressing the importance of intensifying efforts to implement the agreed joint action plans ; stressed the importance of strengthening economic relations with countries and international economic blocs, including through the negotiation of free trade agreements.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Reviewed the results of consultations on the implementation of the decision of the Ministerial Council at its thirty-third session regarding the proposal of the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al Saud to move from the stage of cooperation to the stage of union, and instructed the Ministerial Council to continue efforts towards that transition ; affirmed its interest in the strength and cohesion of the Cooperation Council, the unity of its members and greater coordination, integration and interconnection in all fields, stressing that its countries stand together in the face of any threat to any of the Council's countries.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Congratulated the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the people of Saudi Arabia on winning the right to host the 2034 FIFA World Cup; congratulated the Emir of Kuwait on the successful hosting of the 26th Gulf Cup and Bahrain on winning the trophy; appreciated the UAE's hosting of IDEX and NAVDEX (17-21 February 2025), the 2025 Global Implementation Support Symposium and the 12th World Government Summit; congratulated Bahrain on the 20th Manama Dialogue; appreciated Saudi Arabia's hosting of the 19th Internet Governance Forum; welcomed WIPO's adoption of the "Riyadh Design Law Treaty"; appreciated Oman's 16th Indian Ocean Conference and Qatar's 2024 Doha Forum; welcomed Kuwait's hosting of the Global Humanitarian Overview on 4 December 2024 ; appreciated Bahrain's Islamic-Islamic dialogue conference, welcomed the UN General Assembly's adoption of Bahrain's draft resolution designating 28 January as the International Day of Peaceful Coexistence, and welcomed the second session of the International Conference on Dialogue of Civilizations and Tolerance in Abu Dhabi on 19 February 2025.

a3330.speaker: GCC Ministerial Council (final communique of the 163rd session, Mecca)
a3330.speech: Expressed sincere condolences to the victims of the earthquake in the People's Republic of China, the two air disasters in the Republic of Korea and the Republic of Kazakhstan, the forest fires in the state of California in the United States of America, and the hotel fire in Bolu province in the Republic of Turkey.

a3330.speaker: Arsalan Maleki, Iranian Deputy Minister of Roads and Urban Development
a3330.speech: Statements of 12 May 2024 regarding Iran's intention to grant illegal land and housing projects on the occupied island of Abu Musa.

a3330.speaker: The (late) President of Iran
a3330.speech: Statements of 4 February 2024 during a cabinet session about Iranian industrial efforts on the islands.

a3330.speaker: Mohammad Mokhber, First Vice-President of Iran
a3330.speech: Statements of 11 January 2024 regarding the completion of what he called the Document on the Development of the Three Islands, and what this includes in terms of the construction of housing and projects on the three UAE islands.

a3330.speaker: Ali Akbar Safaei, Iranian Deputy Minister of Roads and Urban Development
a3330.speech: Announcement of 5 November 2024 of the start of construction of 110 housing units on the island of Abu Musa and the opening of the multi-purpose port of Abu Musa.

a3330.speaker: Ahmed al-Sharaa, President of the Syrian Arab Republic
a3330.speech: In his speech of 30 January 2025 he affirmed the new Syrian leadership's commitment to building an inclusive state for all components of the Syrian people, to forming a transitional government in order to establish state institutions in preparation for holding free and fair elections, to launching a National Dialogue Conference and to drafting a new constitution.

a3330.speaker: Joseph Aoun, President of the Lebanese Republic
a3330.speech: His inaugural speech of 9 January 2025 stressed the state's right to restrict weapons, to combat terrorism and smuggling, to preserve the unity of Lebanese territory and Lebanon's Arab identity, to build a strategic partnership with Arab and friendly countries, and rejected any threat to Lebanon's stability and security.

a3330.speaker: King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain
a3330.speech: Initiatives announced at the Arab Summit held in the Kingdom of Bahrain, calling for an international peace conference in the Middle East to establish a national, independent, secure and sovereign Palestinian State, and to support efforts to recognise the Palestinian State internationally and to accept its full membership in the United Nations.

a3330.speaker: Statement of the chair of the Riyadh meetings on Syria, 12 January 2025
a3330.speech: Stressed providing support to the brotherly Syrian people at this important stage and helping to rebuild Syria as a united, independent and secure Arab state, as well as supporting a Syrian political transition process in which the Syrian political and social forces are represented, preserving the rights of all Syrians.

a3335.speaker: Philippe Talavera, Director of the Ombetja Yehinga Organisation (OYO)
a3335.speech: "When the funding from those partners was suspended, it obviously affected us because we are sub-recipients and rely on that money. So it did affect us. And unfortunately, this year, we could only do fewer projects than we normally do. And we could reach many fewer regions than we normally do."

a3335.speaker: Philippe Talavera, Director of the Ombetja Yehinga Organisation (OYO)
a3335.speech: "So it's important to develop the creative sector. But you can only develop the creative sector if people sort of know what it means. For a lot of people, art is a hobby. It's not a job. So we have to start educating people that the creative sector can actually be a job. But as with any job, be it being a doctor, being an engineer, or being a lawyer, it requires training, it requires experience, and it requires exposure. So I think it's important that we encourage young people to explore those opportunities."

a3350.speaker: Adama Sarnor, Executive Director of the Liberia Agency for Community Development (LACD)
a3350.speech: Encourages Liberian farmers not to view themselves as poor, emphasizing that the country's land remains rich despite challenges they face; notes that they are key partners in Liberia's economic development, while stressing the importance of increasing locally produced foods, particularly staples like rice, cassava, eddoes, and yam.

a3350.speaker: Adama Sarnor, Executive Director of the Liberia Agency for Community Development (LACD)
a3350.speech: Says LACD is currently working with approximately 700 smallholder farmers and cooperatives in River Cess County, training them how to plant crops in nurseries to adapt to climate change; acknowledges difficulties some farmers face with this new method, as they are accustomed to traditional farming practices; assures that LACD's experienced staff is providing necessary support to help them adjust, urging farmers to stay focused and determined.

a3350.speaker: Adama Sarnor, Executive Director of the Liberia Agency for Community Development (LACD)
a3350.speech: Highlights LACD's role in promoting food production that addresses poverty and hunger, as well as its collaborations with international partners such as USAID, Irish Aid, Concern Worldwide, and ZOA; expresses gratitude for the trust these partners have placed in LACD over the years; explains that despite challenges of limited resources and heavy reliance on international aid organizations, LACD's mission to implement sustainable programs that will improve education, livelihoods, access to services, and long-term community development is steady; says the vision is to ensure that every community member has the right to survival, protection, healthcare, and participation.

a3350.speaker: Adama Sarnor, Executive Director of the Liberia Agency for Community Development (LACD)
a3350.speech: Calls on fellow NGO leaders in Liberia to be transparent and trustworthy, by ensuring that funds received from international donors are used appropriately for their intended purposes.

a3369.speaker: Vodacom Tanzania (company)
a3369.speech: States that this investment has enabled the launch of modern technologies such as 4G and 5G and has expanded access to high-speed internet to more than 70 percent of the population.

a3369.speaker: Vivienne Penessis, Director of Human Resources at Vodacom Tanzania
a3369.speech: "For eight consecutive years, Vodacom has been recognised as the best employer, and for 13 years there has never been a reported death of an employee at work."

a3399.speaker: Mamo Mihretu, Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
a3399.speech: Claimed a bold reconfiguration of monetary policy and foreign exchange management, marking a break from years of fiscal dominance, closed financial architecture, and constrained market signalling; he told federal legislators last week that the reforms reflect a systemic recalibration that anchors macroeconomic stability, enhances foreign exchange liquidity, and restores credibility to the central banking regime; he recalled a policy rate hike to 15pc and a lending rate to 18pc, moves that signalled tightening to contain inflation and heralded the end of direct monetisation of fiscal deficits, and according to the Governor the structural decoupling of central bank lending to the federal government is seen as a foundation in the central bank's transition toward greater autonomy and inflation-targeting credibility; the Governor projected a 2.6 billion dollar surplus in the overall balance of payments for 2024/25, and a decline of inflation to a single digit next year.

a3399.speaker: Mamo Mihretu, Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
a3399.speech: "We're curbing incentives for capital flight," asserted Governor Mamo, who rejected concerns over the Bank's profitability, arguing a 10 billion Br "unrealised loss" was due to currency depreciation, not operational mismanagement. "There is no such thing as loss. The Bank is not a profit-making institution. It pays high interest when absorbing money from the market."

a3399.speaker: Mamo Mihretu, Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
a3399.speech: Argued that NBE's transformation was further reflected in structural reforms such as a revised banking proclamation that allowed foreign bank entry, the first mobile money license awarded to a foreign investor, and key institutions like the Deposit Insurance Fund and pension agencies reporting digital and regulatory overhauls.

a3399.speaker: Mekbib Tesfaye, London-based analyst
a3399.speech: Observers such as Mekbib Tesfaye have flagged the need for IFRS-compliant asset valuation and transparent reporting: "Fair value mechanisms," he argued, "can restore trust in central bank balance sheets." ; "This is where Ethiopia can take a page from global peers," Mekbib told Fortune. "Central banks in comparable economies have leveraged equity exposure to bolster policy flexibility and manage reserve adequacy."

a3399.speaker: 2024 audit report of the National Bank of Ethiopia
a3399.speech: According to the 2024 audit report, despite booking 26 billion Br in profits, the Bank reported a net forex loss of 28.3 billion Br and raised its impairment provisions by five billion Birr, mostly for loans to state-owned enterprises.

a3399.speaker: Parliament's Budget & Finance Standing Committee, chaired by Desalegn Wedaje
a3399.speech: Raised red flags; members of the committee criticised persistent forex crunch, the widening premium in the parallel market, unattractive deposit rates, liquidity mismatches, and operational inefficiencies in pension funds; MPs also flagged cybersecurity risks, farmers' exclusion from financial services, and pension fund inefficiencies, including low collection rates and a lack of investment planning, as critical bottlenecks; legislators were sceptical about Governor Mamo's bullish forecast of a decline in inflation to a single digit next year.

a3399.speaker: Solomon Desta, Vice Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
a3399.speech: Reiterated the NBE's commitment to inclusive finance, citing the rollout of warehouse financing and green card services in northern regions; he disclosed that a Rural Financial Inclusion Council is also being formed.

a3399.speaker: Girum Ameha, economist
a3399.speech: While lauding reserve gains, warned that 2.7 months' coverage still falls short of the three-month prudential benchmark, and urged diversification beyond gold and coffee exports.

a3399.speaker: Girum Ameha, economist
a3399.speech: Recommended a combination of targeted incentives and reforming the commission structure that banks earn from facilitating remittances, to close the import-export gap and boost official remittance flows: "Flat caps on commissions don't work, banks should be rewarded for performance," he said; he warned that bureaucratic bottlenecks are nudging users toward the informal market ; on treasury bond policy, following the National Bank's directive requiring banks to purchase government securities: "If bonds are to fill the deficit gap, they must be priced to attract," Girum argued; the existing bulk-purchase structure, he said, adds to investor hesitation; still, with the advent of capital market trading, he remains optimistic: "Wealthy investors will show up if the returns are worthwhile," he said.

a3399.speaker: Ameha Tefera (PhD), veteran banker
a3399.speech: Labelled the fuel subsidy removal decision "economic sabotage," despite the government's push for cost-reflective pricing. "Our dependence on imports is a huge loss," he told Fortune. "There's a huge gap between what we import and export."

a3399.speaker: Experts (unnamed)
a3399.speech: Questioned the sustainability of foreign liabilities, such as Abu Dhabi's deposits ballooning to 174 billion Br at a rate of four per cent interest, with projections revealing these could swell to 390 billion Br with further Birr depreciation, causing latent fiscal exposure; experts also say vulnerabilities remain - inflation control is elusive, the forex premium with the parallel market persists, and the Central Bank's 430 billion Br in sub-market loans to government agencies presents long-term fiscal risks - and say whether these reforms coalesce into a sustainable framework remains an open question.

a3474.speaker: Neil Postman, information theorist
a3474.speech: Addressing the nascent computer industry in 1990, questioned the unspoken assumption that the capacity to process information is at the heart of society's ills: “If children die of starvation in Ethiopia, does it occur because of a lack of information?” he asked. “Does racism in South Africa exist because of a lack of information? If criminals roam the streets of New York City, do they do so because of a lack of information?”

a3474.speaker: Johann Rupert, South Africa's richest man
a3474.speech: In the Oval Office meeting between President Donald Trump and President Cyril Ramaphosa and his delegation, pleaded the case that the country's police stations are in desperate need of Starlink — the communication technology controlled by Elon Musk ; articulated the fact that crime is devastating to the whole nation, and not one group in particular, and used the Western Cape as an example of its complexity.

a3604.speaker: Succès Masra, Prime Minister of Chad
a3604.speech: assured that an “international-type investigation” to “establish responsibilities” would be opened. “The government has committed to conducting an international-type investigation that will make it possible to establish responsibilities at all levels. There are photos, but there is also a film, the film of the events. I would like to invite everyone to watch the film of all the events,” the Prime Minister declared.

a3620.speaker: Mark Christopher Toner, United States Ambassador to Liberia
a3620.speech: Highlighted the importance of continued U.S.-Liberia partnership in public health, emphasizing the United States’ long-standing commitment to bolstering Liberia’s ability to detect and treat infectious diseases.

a3620.speaker: Representatives of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
a3620.speech: Were also present to reaffirm support for Liberia’s public health infrastructure.

a3620.speaker: U.S. Embassy in Liberia (official Facebook post)
a3620.speech: Posted that “Liberia is an important global health security partner for the U.S. in West Africa.” The statement further highlighted NPHIL’s significant role since its establishment in 2016, and how the U.S. government has been a proud contributor to NPHIL’s mission of preventing infectious disease outbreaks and improving the country’s health systems.

a3620.speaker: Zinnah Emrys Koisee, social media user
a3620.speech: Thanked the United States for its “continued support towards our health system.”

a3620.speaker: Ebenezer Steve Morlia, social media user
a3620.speech: Expressed confidence in Dr. Nyan’s leadership, stating that “Dr. Nyan will lead the charge and make immense impacts at NPHIL.”

a3620.speaker: Watson Chelley, social media user
a3620.speech: Added, “Positive work Ambassador. Liberia needs more financial support from the U.S. government. We have infrastructure, human resources, and technology challenges.”

a3620.speaker: Dr. Dougbeh Chris Nyan, Director-General of the National Public Health Institute of Liberia (NPHIL)
a3620.speech: During a press conference at NPHIL headquarters on October 13, 2024, confirmed the presence of three new cases of Mpox, bringing the total number of cases to eleven since the virus was declared a Public Health Emergency by Africa CDC and the WHO in August 2024: “Knowledge of the Mpox Clade-Ila circulating in Liberia provides critical scientific insight on how the virus spreads and how we can enhance our diagnostics, vaccine strategy, and overall response to the outbreak.” ; Urged the public to remain calm, practice good hygiene, and report any suspected cases to health authorities.

a3647.speaker: Civil society organisations (CSOs) and human rights activists
a3647.speech: Have said they are not shaken by United States of America President Donald Trump's order to stop support towards reproductive health rights issues; have proposed identification of sustainable ways to finance initiatives in the sector locally; said in Lilongwe on Friday that even without the US support, various safe abortion campaigns will proceed in the country.

a3647.speaker: Michael Kaiyatsa, executive director, Centre for Human Rights and Rehabilitation
a3647.speech: Said while the CSO leaders and activists agree that Trump's order will have a ripple effect, the aid freeze is an opportunity for reflection on how best they can run their campaigns without depending on US funding, and serves as a reminder of the urgent need to stand firm in their commitment to promote reproductive justice ; “We are at a critical juncture where our collective action can make a difference. This meeting is not merely an exchange of information, it is a call to action. By sharing our insights, experiences, and strategies, we can empower one another to face opposition with confidence and creativity.”

a3647.speaker: Godfrey Kangaunde, executive director, Nyale Institute
a3647.speech: Acknowledged the impact of Trump's order, saying this is a wake-up call for rights activists to rethink donor dependence, and said that without USAid funding there will be limited resources available for advancing the safe abortion campaign in Malawi ; “With the US now shifting its stance, we must ask: Can we find sustainable alternatives within Malawi and Africa? Should we let this change set us back, or can we find new, local sources of support?”

a3647.speaker: Emma Kaliya, gender activist and chair of the Coalition for Prevention of Unsafe Abortion (Copua)
a3647.speech: Said Trump does not speak for the whole world and, therefore, sovereign States can still carry on the advocacy.

a3903.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3903.speech: Declared in a video clip that henceforth in the USA its citizens would only be recognized as belonging to two sexes: male and female.

a3903.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3903.speech: “We have had very serious problems with Christians who are being murdered in Nigeria,” Mr Trump blurted out at his first meeting with President Muhammadu Buhari. “We are going to be working on that problem very, very hard because we cannot allow that to happen.”

a3903.speaker: BBC analyst
a3903.speech: Remarked that this was a strategy Trump deployed to please his persecuted audience: “But perhaps it should not come as any surprise. Mr Trump has always been quick to jump to the defence of Christians in conflicts such as Syria and Iraq and comments like this play well to his base among Evangelical Christians in the US.”

a3923.speaker: Adeyombo Aderinto, California-based friend of the writer
a3923.speech: Wrote a tribute to Ngugi wa Thiong'o that alerted the writer, on Thursday, May 29th, 2025, to the passing of that giant of African writing.

a3923.speaker: Okey Ndibe
a3923.speech: Published a short tribute to Ngugi wa Thiong'o and a galaxy of pictures that he had taken over the years with Ngugi.

a3923.speaker: Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Kenyan writer
a3923.speech: Had begun a process of interrogation of what he described as "the general bourgeois education system" in Kenya before his detention, including efforts at "demystifying" theatrical performances.

a3923.speaker: Friedrich Engels
a3923.speech: As Fredrich Engels said in his funeral oration for Karl Marx, mankind was a head shorter with his passing.

a4044.speaker: Tatyana Dovgalenko, head of the Department for Partnership with Africa at the Russian Foreign Ministry
a4044.speech: Said in an interview with RIA Novosti that due to sanctions, Russia was unable to send money for food aid to African countries such as Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger and Sudan in 2024. According to her, Russia provides humanitarian assistance to African countries in need both through bilateral channels and through international organizations, including the United Nations World Food Program (WFP), which she said is a key multilateral channel for Moscow to provide such assistance. "The Government of the Russian Federation has allocated the necessary financing to the program for the supply of domestic food to Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger and Sudan. However, due to the sanctions imposed by Washington in November 2024 against Russian financial institutions, including those that serve our donor projects in international organizations, it has not yet been possible to transfer funds." She recalled that Russia has been sending an annual contribution of $10 million to WFP since 2020, and last year was no exception.

a4044.speaker: Tatyana Dovgalenko, head of the Department for Partnership with Africa at the Russian Foreign Ministry
a4044.speech: "This situation clearly illustrates the falsity of Western statements about the so-called 'humanitarian exemptions' and the 'targeted' nature of illegal unilateral restrictions against Russia." She stressed that Moscow is taking steps to find a solution to these problems, and as soon as the issue of transferring Russian donor funds is resolved, the WFP will coordinate with the national governments of the beneficiary countries the nomenclature of the necessary food, and suppliers will satisfy these requests.

a4235.speaker: Moumina Okieh, president of the IFTIN association
a4235.speech: Described this initiative as a success; stressed that the women who participated in the various training sessions had assimilated valuable knowledge and renewed motivation; ended her intervention by saying that the IFTIN ALI-SABIEH Association continues to play a key role in community development, proving once again its dedication and its effectiveness.

a4235.speaker: Aden Abdillahi Ali, secretary general of the regional council
a4235.speech: Congratulated the members of the association for their commitment to actions of a social character.

a4235.speaker: Beneficiaries of the drinking-water tanks
a4235.speech: Thanked the members of the IFTIN association: a handover of containers “that will strengthen our storage capacity for the precious liquid and that comes in the middle of the hot season.”

a4534.speaker: United States Embassy in Tanzania
a4534.speech: Has confirmed that development projects that were being implemented through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) will be restored, despite the agency having been closed earlier this year.

a4534.speaker: Andrew Lentz, acting US Ambassador (Chargé d’Affaires) to Tanzania
a4534.speech: Said, speaking to journalists in Arusha on Sunday, September 14, 2025, that the closure of USAID does not mean the end of development projects, but that there will be a new implementation framework to ensure the projects continue; explained that the United States will work with various organisations and local communities to take on responsibility for managing some of the projects that were under USAID: “We will ensure the projects are carried out again in collaboration with local and international stakeholders. Our goal is to advance conservation efforts and social development.”

a4534.speaker: World Wildlife Fund (WWF)
a4534.speech: Has expressed hope that the move to restore those projects could go hand in hand with the return of funding through the United States Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC).

a4577.speaker: Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) (statistics)
a4577.speech: According to INEC statistics, most appeals are decided within a period of less than one week, but this also depends on the weight of the arguments in each appeal.

a4577.speaker: Tanzania Political Research Organisation (2021 study)
a4577.speech: Showed that 40 percent of candidates who were rejected by electoral commissions fell into depression after their appeals failed.

a4577.speaker: Police Force (2019 statistics)
a4577.speech: Show that 60 percent of the violence reported during the local government elections was caused by supporters who were dissatisfied with the results of their candidates' appeals.

a4577.speaker: University of Dar es Salaam (UDSM) (2021 research)
a4577.speech: Found that candidates who build a positive image in society through their words and deeds have a greater chance of obtaining lasting support even after the election.

a4577.speaker: USAID (international aid and development agency)
a4577.speech: According to USAID, 45 percent of candidates who involve themselves in volunteer activities in the community increased their support in future elections.

a4577.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a4577.speech: Indicates that 15 percent of people who take part in politics have high levels of stress, especially while waiting for important results such as these.

a4577.speaker: Centre for Democracy and Development (2022 research)
a4577.speech: Shows that 70 percent of candidates who went through appeals came back with firmer plans and better strategies for taking part in future elections.

a4577.speaker: Institute of Political and Democratic Affairs (TPDI) (2021 research)
a4577.speech: Found that 35 percent of candidates who cooperated with key stakeholders obtained a good chance of gaining support over a long period, despite the challenges they encountered during the election.

a4577.speaker: Leadership Ethics Research Organisation (SOMU) (2022 statistics)
a4577.speech: Show that 55 percent of voters are more likely to support a candidate who shows integrity, even after losing in earlier elections.

a4708.speaker: UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)
a4708.speech: Reported today that the first delivery was 150 tonnes, out of a total of 1,500 tonnes, which will go to 2,450 families dedicated to raising and caring for livestock in the Gaza Strip; said the organisation intends to deliver, in a first phase, a total of 1,500 tonnes of fodder, enough to produce and supply milk for 50 days to all children in Gaza under 10 years old, already covering about 20% of the minimum daily requirements recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) in terms of calories.

a4708.speaker: Ciro Fiorillo, director of the FAO unit in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip
a4708.speech: "Every animal that dies causes lasting impacts, since replacing it is expensive and practically impossible because of import restrictions." ; "By ensuring the availability of fodder, we can support the survival and reproduction of livestock and supply essential, fresh and nutritious food, even during conflicts."

a4708.speaker: UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)
a4708.speech: Noted that this is the first time since the escalation of hostilities in the small, overcrowded Palestinian enclave that fodder has entered Gaza, the restrictions having "caused the collapse of agri-food value chains, contributing to the rapid deterioration of food security"; added that since the start of the conflict on 7 October 2023, 55% of the animals linked to the supply of meat and milk in the Gaza Strip have been slaughtered, consumed or lost and that, in March, only about 30,000 remained.

a4708.speaker: UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)
a4708.speech: Committed to expanding its aid by providing "crucial agricultural support to restore the availability of highly nutritious food, avoid the total collapse of the sector, preserve the remaining livelihoods and reduce acute hunger and malnutrition".

a4708.speaker: International community
a4708.speech: Has appealed on various occasions to Israel to allow a greater quantity of humanitarian aid to enter the Gaza Strip, especially in the north of the enclave, where the situation is most serious.

a4708.speaker: Israeli authorities
a4708.speech: According to the Israeli authorities, the Hamas attack on Israeli soil of 7 October 2023 caused about 1,200 deaths and two hundred hostages.

a4708.speaker: Hamas
a4708.speech: According to Hamas, which has governed the small Palestinian enclave since 2007, the Israeli offensive in the Gaza Strip has caused more than 33,000 deaths.

a4708.speaker: United Nations (UN)
a4708.speech: Described the more than 1.1 million people in a "catastrophic hunger situation" as "the highest number ever recorded" by the UN in studies on food security in the world.

a4765.speaker: Kazie Uko, the governor's former Chief Press Secretary (statement during the commissioning)
a4765.speech: “Abia State Governor, Dr. Alex Otti, has continued to match words with action with the formal commissioning of three-newly reconstructed roads in Aba. The roads are Udeagbala Road, Umuimo Road and MCC/Old Express Road. Governor Otti described the three roads as strategic, saying that the Udeagbala and Umuimo roads in particular are more or less alternative from the Enugu-Port Harcourt Expressway into the busy Aba-Owerri Road and to Abia State University Teaching Hospital (ABSUTH) road, while the MCC/Old Express Road would boost the economy of Aba, the commercial nerve centre of the State.”

a4765.speaker: Residents of the community
a4765.speech: Have expressed deep concerns over the failure of the newly rehabilitated road and drainage system.

a4765.speaker: Residents of the community
a4765.speech: Many have reported having to wait until floodwaters subside before leaving their homes, especially after rainfalls.

a4765.speaker: Possible Nwaohamuo, community member (live video broadcast)
a4765.speech: Made an appeal to the state government, urging immediate intervention, and pointed out that the floodwaters from the failed drainage system have not only taken over homes but have also severely affected schools and places of worship in the area ; “The flooding is a disaster for our community. We can no longer go about our daily activities in peace. Our children cannot go to school, and our places of worship are submerged. We need the government to come to our rescue. Despite the rehabilitation project being relatively new, its failure has raised questions about the quality of work done and the long-term sustainability of such projects.”

a4783.speaker: Evariste Ndayishimiye, President of the Republic of Burundi
a4783.speech: Called on economic operators to work in unity, transparency and honesty ; urged Burundian economic operators and investors to adopt a forward-looking vision, prioritising the creation of production companies offering goods for export rather than limiting themselves to imports ; insisted that Burundians must take advantage of the peace and security currently prevailing in the country, fundamental elements for development, and recalled that Burundi's progress rests on the commitment of its citizens.

a4783.speaker: Evariste Ndayishimiye, President of the Republic of Burundi
a4783.speech: Called on economic operators not to rely solely on foreign aid, insisting on the importance of collective work and unity in building a strong economy.

a4783.speaker: Evariste Ndayishimiye, President of the Republic of Burundi
a4783.speech: Appealed to all economic actors to renounce fraudulent practices in the fiscal domain, underlining their negative impact on the country's growth ; called on economic operators to pay their taxes and duties in accordance with the law, stressing that these contributions are essential to the country's development, since tax revenues finance electricity production, the purchase of medicines, infrastructure development and many other vital sectors ; urged them to strengthen value chains to facilitate access to raw materials and promote sustainable collective development.

a4783.speaker: Evariste Ndayishimiye, President of the Republic of Burundi
a4783.speech: Deplored certain practices aimed at destabilising the national economy, saying that although foreign currency is available in sufficient quantity in the country, some Burundians manoeuvre to prevent it from entering the Central Bank and the commercial banks; called for a change of mentality and a patriotic spirit focused on the country's development, affirming that Burundi can only prosper with the active involvement of its citizens, failing which it risks sinking into economic decline.

a4783.speaker: Révérien Nizigiyimana, Director General of the ADB (Burundi Development Agency)
a4783.speech: Invites Burundian economic operators to become producers of foreign currency rather than merely requesting it; encourages them to adopt a broader vision, taking an interest not only in the local market but also in the foreign market; stresses the importance of economies of scale, suggesting that entrepreneurs pool their capital in order to create large companies competitive at the international level.

a4783.speaker: Olivier Suguru, President of the CFCIB (Federal Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Burundi)
a4783.speech: Welcomed the Head of State's willingness to encourage economic operators, as shown by the meetings he organises to strengthen dialogue between the public and private sectors; recalled that the CFCIB's mission is to intervene in cases of violations of private-sector rights and not to resolve disputes involving private-sector members or operators who have broken the law, and that any offender must answer for their acts before the competent courts.

a4783.speaker: Olivier Suguru, President of the CFCIB (Federal Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Burundi)
a4783.speech: Firmly denounces economic operators who engage in customs and tax fraud and urges them to put an end to these bad practices, which hinder the broadening of the tax base and impede the country's development; says tax fraud leads to the evasion of income tax, creating an imbalance in the national economy and in trade, and that this fraud often operates as a chain involving certain customs and police officers ; calls on everyone to denounce these practices harmful to the country's development.

a4783.speaker: CFCIB (Federal Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Burundi)
a4783.speech: Is calling for urgent measures to improve the availability of foreign currency and to clean up the business environment in Burundi.

a4783.speaker: Olivier Suguru, President of the CFCIB
a4783.speech: Warns that this problem could have serious consequences for the national economy, notably because of the calculation of taxes based on the exchange rate of the BRB (Bank of the Republic of Burundi).

a4802.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP) (statement)
a4802.speech: Said on Tuesday that it had provided life-saving assistance to one million people affected by “a complex humanitarian crisis” in Burkina Faso, made possible thanks to a contribution of 124 million dollars from USAID, representing 70% of all donor contributions to the WFP office for Burkina Faso in 2024; the UN agency specified in a statement that this contribution comprises 99 million dollars as emergency food assistance and 25 million dollars for the United Nations Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS).

a4802.speaker: Sory Ouane, WFP Representative in Burkina Faso
a4802.speech: “At a time of growing global crisis, this unwavering support has enabled WFP to reach people in need in hard-to-reach places in Burkina Faso” ; “We are deeply grateful for the partnership and the trust that the American government has placed in us.”

a4802.speaker: Cadre Harmonisé food security analysis of March 2024
a4802.speech: According to it, an estimated 2.7 million people – or 12% of the population – needed immediate food assistance during the lean season from June to August 2024.

a5041.speaker: IMF directors
a5041.speech: Have signalled their interest in providing Ethiopia with up to 3.5 billion dollars in loans.

a5041.speaker: Mamo Mihretu, Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
a5041.speech: "Discussions took place and will continue to occur," declining to comment on details of the discussions with the IMF.

a5041.speaker: Mamo Mihretu, Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
a5041.speech: Said the central bank is committed to maintaining stable prices with a single-digit inflation rate, promoting financial inclusion and restructuring the central bank under a new proclamation soon, regardless of external support, and that the National Bank of Ethiopia's three-year strategic plan guides these actions.

a5041.speaker: Tobias N. Rasmussen, IMF resident representative in Ethiopia
a5041.speech: Declined to comment: "We cannot answer these questions as negotiations are ongoing," he responded by email to questions Fortune forwarded to his office.

a5041.speaker: People informed of the ongoing talks (anonymous)
a5041.speech: Point to the liberalisation of the forex regime, discipline over off-budget spending, tax reforms, and the restructuring of high debts held by state enterprises as contentious issues between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's administration and the IMF.

a5041.speaker: IMF team
a5041.speech: Argue that liberalisation of the forex regime, discipline over off-budget spending, tax reforms and restructuring of state enterprise debt are crucial steps to restore macroeconomic stability.

a5041.speaker: Experts
a5041.speech: Say that while loans and debt restructuring offer a lifeline, implementing the reforms the IMF pushes will be critical to achieving sustainable economic growth, and pose the question of what comes next for a country with foreign currency sufficient to cover only three weeks of imports, over 20 million people in need of humanitarian assistance, and security concerns impeding economic productivity.

a5041.speaker: UNDP (projections)
a5041.speech: Projected that Ethiopia's debt service costs will reach four billion dollars in two years.

a5041.speaker: A macroeconomist (anonymous)
a5041.speech: Likened the IMF program to an ambulance providing immediate assistance, with long-term health dependent on sustained attention to overall well-being: "Tough but essential measures are what the program offers." ; praised the central bank's current orientation and urged strong, sound, and resilient reforms, saying countries benefiting from IMF programs must leverage the potential credit facility to address structural economic imbalances effectively - "It's timely and encouraging."

a5041.speaker: Abiy Ahmed, Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a5041.speech: Recently likened reforms to a dentist pulling out a tooth, signalling the need for strict measures, and hinted at forthcoming reforms.

a5041.speaker: People familiar with the ongoing talks (anonymous)
a5041.speech: Say Ethiopia's authorities have agreed on the reform measures to be taken in principle, and that the bone of contention with the IMF is over extended time and phased implementation deals they call "back-loaded," while the IMF team insisted on "front-loaded" deals.

a5041.speaker: Atlaw Alemu (PhD), economist
a5041.speech: Downplayed the significance of either a slight currency devaluation or a significant shift in exchange rate policy for the main economy, viewing the economic turmoil as stemming from deeper systemic failures rather than exchange rate policies, and noted that past devaluations, including a 15pc drop six years ago, did little to improve export performance or bolster foreign currency reserves: "Exchange rate policy is a smaller element of the country's economic problems." ; said the agricultural export sector, reliant on imports for inputs like fertiliser and seeds, will struggle with higher costs regardless of exchange rate adjustments, and that unlike China, Ethiopia's productivity levels have not improved significantly.

a5041.speaker: Atlaw Alemu (PhD), economist
a5041.speech: Suggested that while the IMF program could somewhat relieve debt burdens, it may not address the root causes of the economic malaise: "A path to a little debt relief is all the IMF could offer."

a5227.speaker: Somali Journalists Syndicate (SJS)
a5227.speech: strongly condemns the unlawful arrest of two journalists in Adaado town, Galmudug State, on Tuesday, 5 August 2025, following their reporting on the alleged rape and murder of an eight-year-old girl in Adaado town.

a5227.speaker: Reports on female genital mutilation prevalence
a5227.speech: Reports estimate national prevalence of female genital mutilation (FGM) among women aged 15–49 in Somalia to be 99.2%.

a5227.speaker: Formal Complaint Against Speaker of the Federal Parliament of Somalia, Sheikh Aadan Mohamed Nur (Aadan Madoobe) (document)
a5227.speech: Subject: Formal Complaint Against Speaker of the Federal Parliament of Somalia, Sheikh Aadan Mohamed Nur (Aadan Madoobe) – Abuse of Power, Community Persecution, and State-Sanctioned Repression.

a5227.speaker: Residents of the Kabaase camp for internally displaced Somalis near Doolow
a5227.speech: citing extreme food shortages, lack of healthcare, and growing despair due to aid suspensions and worsening security conditions.

a5227.speaker: Somali Journalists Syndicate (SJS) and its network of members
a5227.speech: proudly congratulate its Secretary General, Abdalle Ahmed Mumin, for receiving an Honourable Mention at the 2025 Allard Prize for International Integrity.

a5227.speaker: Somali Media Association (SOMA)
a5227.speech: welcomes the recent high-level meeting between civil society leaders and the European Union Ambassador to Somalia, H.E. Karin Johansson.

a5315.speaker: Panelists at the World Food Day event (Liberian food system actors)
a5315.speech: Underscored the need for a transformative agriculture and mentioned the need for the government to exert more efforts to address pertinent issues that still confront the country's agriculture and food system, outlining ensuring women's access to land, improving extension services, improving access to finance and the provision of adequate inputs among others as some critical issues; they said that addressing those issues will inspire more young farmers and agripreneurs to set out in exploring opportunities in the agriculture and agribusiness sector.

a5315.speaker: Hawa Dunor Varney, Executive Director for Women In Agriculture
a5315.speech: Said that women contribute immensely to the food system in Liberia and as such there is need for the government to continue to create the enabling environment to improve farming; said that as an organization, considering the difficulties women experience in access to land, they are working to create awareness around the issue: "We are providing the skills and knowledge as well as providing them the education on business knowledge to make agriculture a business. We are also providing literacy education as part of our programs so that the women can go out and seek for opportunities" ; "As an organization we advocate women access to land in communities to be able to provide land to grow their food."

a5315.speaker: Hired Lankah, of Nimba Venture, a snail farmer
a5315.speech: Explained that his organization is working to change the mindset of young people about agriculture: "We provide not just food security but also alternative livelihood. I try to make the young people understand that agriculture requires developing the proper mindset to succeed" ; he mentioned that there are a lot of challenges that still confront snail farming and so they are supporting young people who don't have the starting capital.

a5315.speaker: Neemu Barcom of the Farmer Union Network of Liberia
a5315.speech: Explained that her organization has been very much busy addressing post-harvest losses in the food sector: "We also worked to train farmers in the past for rice cultivation," adding that her organization currently works to revamp the coffee sector, that the program aims to train farmers in improved coffee cultivation to improve incomes, that though the project is yet to provide equipment farmers are trained in harvest and processing, and that for the first time under the program farmers were able to export some quantities of coffee to Europe: "The farmers are very much excited about the program as more women and youths are now getting involved."

a5590.speaker: Jean-Claude Kassi Brou, Governor of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO)
a5590.speech: Stressed economic priorities within the WAEMU area and called for strengthened global cooperation as the only way to meet the region's challenges of rising debt, climate risks, insecurity and youth employment.

a5590.speaker: Jean-Claude Kassi Brou, Governor of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO)
a5590.speech: Insisted on the macroeconomic stability needed to support regional growth despite external shocks: "The resilience of our economy rests on appropriate fiscal and monetary policy, particularly in a context of global economic volatility," citing the repercussions of climate change, debt and insecurity in the region.

a5590.speaker: Jean-Claude Kassi Brou, Governor of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO)
a5590.speech: "It is becoming essential to establish mechanisms to better manage this debt and reduce the risk of over-indebtedness" ; proposed better coordination between international financial institutions and regional institutions in order to put in place innovative financial instruments responding to the specific needs of African countries.

a5590.speaker: Jean-Claude Kassi Brou, Governor of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO)
a5590.speech: Stated that climate variations directly influence economic growth and increase vulnerabilities in health and employment: "We must step up our efforts to integrate climate resilience strategies into our economic policies" ; called for a mobilisation of international resources to finance resilient infrastructure and strengthen local capacities to mitigate climate effects.

a5590.speaker: Jean-Claude Kassi Brou, Governor of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO)
a5590.speech: Insisted on the need for a balanced approach in the allocation of public resources: "Strengthened security is essential to protect infrastructure and encourage foreign investment, but it must not compromise the financing of social and economic development."

a5590.speaker: Jean-Claude Kassi Brou, Governor of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO)
a5590.speech: Underlined the importance of strengthening human capital and creating job opportunities adapted to market needs: "The employment challenge is urgent. We must explore strategies that promote the professional integration of young people, notably through entrepreneurship and digitalisation," calling for greater engagement from international actors to support employment initiatives in emerging economies.

a5590.speaker: BCEAO (data)
a5590.speech: According to data provided by the BCEAO, between 1980 and 2022 climate disasters affected more than 80 million people in the WAEMU zone.

a5590.speaker: Latest data (cited)
a5590.speech: According to the latest data, public external debt in sub-Saharan Africa quadrupled in less than two decades, rising from $108 billion in 2006 to $462 billion in 2022.

a5755.speaker: World Bank (Africa's Pulse report)
a5755.speech: Said economic activity in Sub-Saharan Africa is projected to edge up from 3.3 per cent in 2024 to 3.5 per cent in 2025 and further accelerate to 4.3 per cent in 2026-27, but that the region's economic performance is still dragged down by some of its largest countries - namely, Angola, Nigeria, and South Africa ; “Excluding these countries, the rest of the subcontinent is expected to grow at 4.6 per cent in 2025 and speed up to 5.7 percent in 2026–27. This outlook is subject to heightened risks arising from global policy uncertainty” ; “As inflation cools down and converges to targets, and (global and domestic) financial conditions remain accommodative, it is expected that household consumption and investment will support the region’s growth acceleration” ; said the contribution of government consumption will remain modest as the public sector continues to balance revenues and expenditures while managing painful trade-offs between servicing the debt burden and investing in social and physical infrastructure, and that the contribution of services is expected to remain robust in 2025–27

a5755.speaker: World Bank (Africa's Pulse report)
a5755.speech: “Sub-Saharan African economies will navigate an uncertain landscape amid greater policy uncertainty, which may lead to changes in the world trade order; ongoing (regional and national) geopolitical shifts that may affect commodity prices, disrupt international relations, and yield further fragmentation; reduced foreign aid budgets worldwide; and challenges posed by extreme weather events.”

a5755.speaker: World Bank (Africa's Pulse report)
a5755.speech: Said that in per capita terms, growth in the region has been inadequate to yield significant reductions in extreme poverty; that forecasts indicate that after reaching a peak of 43.9 per cent in 2025, poverty, measured at $2.15 per capita per day in 2017 international purchasing power parity, will drop to 43.2 percent in 2027; and that limited investments in income-generating sectors for the poor, lingering effects of past inflation, and the probable reduction of donor aid budgets worldwide pose a challenge for poverty reduction

a5755.speaker: World Bank (Africa's Pulse report)
a5755.speech: Said the median inflation rate in Sub-Saharan Africa declined from 7.1 per cent in 2023 to 4.5 per cent in 2024, and is projected to bounce back slightly to an annual average rate of 4.6 per cent in 2025–27 ; “However, the variability of inflation across countries remains high: of 47 countries in the region, 14 still have inflation rates of two digits or more—including Angola, Ethiopia, Ghana, Malawi, Nigeria, Sudan, and Zimbabwe, among others” ; “By 2027, the number of countries with two-digit or higher inflation rates is expected to fall to six.”

a5959.speaker: Ambassador Dahir Arab, Somalia’s Ambassador to the United States
a5959.speech: Said that they have sat down with the US Government several times and that there is no near-term or long-term plan for it to recognise Somaliland as a state independent from the rest of Somalia: “That matter would give rise to responsibilities and obligations that it is difficult to rush into, and it is even harder to find anyone who would dare take on such a great error.”

a5959.speaker: Ambassador Dahir Arab, Somalia’s Ambassador to the United States (interview with VOA Somali Service)
a5959.speech: Disclosed that the Government of Somalia will request the United States to give USAID aid directly to the Government, whereas it was previously channelled through local agencies or NGOs: “The US Government supports us with the logistics of the Danab forces and their salaries, and we will directly request that USAID aid be given directly to the Federal Government.”

a5959.speaker: Members of the Republican Party (unnamed)
a5959.speech: Said that Trump’s plan for this year, 2025, includes recognising Somaliland as an independent state.

a6250.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)
a6250.speech: Said only 350,000 people will receive food assistance in November, down from 1.1 million in August, meaning it can now reach just one in every ten people in urgent need of help to survive.

a6250.speaker: Ross Smith, WFP's Director of Emergency Preparedness and Response
a6250.speech: “We are seeing a dangerous rise in emergency levels of hunger, and our ability to respond is shrinking by the day” ; “Without urgent funding, families already pushed to the edge will be left with nothing at a time when they need it most.”

a6250.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) latest report
a6250.speech: According to the latest IPC, 4.6 million Somalis face crisis levels of food insecurity or worse (IPC Phase 3+), with nearly 1 million people enduring emergency conditions (IPC 4).

a6250.speaker: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)
a6250.speech: Estimates 1.8 million children under five are acutely malnourished, including 421,000 suffering from severe malnutrition.

a6250.speaker: Humanitarian agencies
a6250.speech: Say reduced donor support and U.S. foreign aid cuts enacted under the Rescissions Act of 2025, which rescinded nearly $8 billion in global assistance, have further strained response efforts, leaving organizations like WFP operating well below required levels.

a6250.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)
a6250.speech: Said it urgently needs $98 million to sustain a minimum level of life-saving operations for 800,000 people through the upcoming lean season, which extends to March 2026.

a6250.speaker: Humanitarian experts
a6250.speech: Warn that without new funding, Somalia risks sliding into catastrophic hunger conditions reminiscent of the 2011 famine, when more than 250,000 people died.

a6415.speaker: Tony O. Elumelu, African business leader, chairman of Heirs Holdings
a6415.speech: Called on business leaders from the BRICS countries to make room for African companies seeking to expand beyond the continent into the BRICS, and spoke of the need for mutually beneficial partnerships between African countries and the BRICS: "We are witnessing the emergence of a new generation of entrepreneurs whose ambitions extend beyond the continent. They should invest in the BRICS in the same way that the BRICS invest in Africa; this relationship must be a two-way street." ; Concluded: "As African business leaders, and as Africapitalists, we agree that we possess sufficient resources to move things forward in Africa. We must share the opportunities on the continent. We are numerous enough to make a difference. We must work together to find ways of increasing trade and investment links between the BRICS and Africa."

a6415.speaker: Donald Kaberuka, President of the African Development Bank
a6415.speech: Stressed the need to improve infrastructure on the continent, asserting that businesses can only prosper if the infrastructure deficit problem is solved.

a6415.speaker: Isabella Dos Santos, Angolan investor
a6415.speech: Emphasised the need for investment in "intangible" infrastructure, arguing that broadband technology would have a transformative effect similar to that of mobile technology in Africa.

a6415.speaker: Mo Ibrahim, founder of the Mo Ibrahim Foundation
a6415.speech: Spoke about the poor image of Africa at the global level and the importance of governance, and about his foundation's governance index, one of the most comprehensive in the world, measuring 88 parameters including transparency, corruption, education and health. His final message to investors was: "Do not come to Africa to help and make money, because the best return on investment is in Africa. You may enjoy making money in Africa but, please, be responsible."

a6415.speaker: Johann Rupert, South African businessman, chairman of Richemont and Remgro
a6415.speech: Spoke about the essential factors he considers as an investor, wherever his investments are located, listing four critical areas: the rule of law, the independence of the judicial system, the security of property, and the transparency of markets.

a6444.speaker: Rev. Baxton Maulidi, economic justice and accountability champion for the All Africa Conference of Churches (AACC) in Malawi
a6444.speech: Urged the Malawi government to prioritize transparency and accountability throughout the 2025 General Elections process to prevent suspicions of electoral malpractice ; faulted the government for failing to provide regular updates on the NRB's operations at Kanengo, which he said could have avoided the ensuing controversy: "It is clear that many Malawians were unaware of this arrangement. The lack of communication has created unnecessary suspicion. Ahead of the elections, transparency and regular updates are critical to maintaining public trust."

a6444.speaker: Rev. Baxton Maulidi, economic justice and accountability champion for the All Africa Conference of Churches (AACC) in Malawi
a6444.speech: Emphasized that security is a key component of electoral transparency, noting that the absence of law enforcement at the Kanengo facility allowed the MPs to make potentially misleading accusations: "Part of transparency is ensuring that sensitive facilities like the Kanengo warehouse are secure. Without proper security, allegations of electoral malpractice will persist, whether true or not."

a6444.speaker: Rev. Baxton Maulidi, economic justice and accountability champion for the All Africa Conference of Churches (AACC) in Malawi
a6444.speech: Called for collaborative efforts by the government, electoral stakeholders, and development partners to regularly inform the public about the progress of voter registration and other electoral processes: "Transparency must be at the core of every stage of the electoral process. The government and its partners should proactively share information to dispel any suspicions. This would prevent situations like the Kanengo incident from escalating." ; also urged whistleblowers to act responsibly, ensuring that allegations are backed by evidence to avoid creating panic or undermining public confidence in the electoral process ; concluded by reiterating that transparency, accountability, and security must go hand-in-hand to safeguard Malawi's democracy and the integrity of the 2025 elections.

a6444.speaker: George Chaponda, Leader of the Opposition
a6444.speech: Accused the government of colluding with the National Registration Bureau (NRB) to compromise voter registration, following a surprise visit by Chaponda and opposition MPs to a National Food Reserve Agency (NFRA) warehouse in Kanengo, Lilongwe, where the NRB operates a satellite facility ; alleged the facility was being used for suspicious activities after finding thousands of national IDs on the warehouse floor, some packed in sacks.

a6444.speaker: National Registration Bureau (NRB)
a6444.speech: Clarified that the facility was part of a 2017 arrangement supported by international development partners, including the UNDP, EU, and USAID, to ensure continuous national registration and efficient distribution of IDs.

a6484.speaker: Integrity Watch-Liberia
a6484.speech: Has stressed the need for all hands to get on deck to harness efforts aimed at curbing corruption, increasing accountability and strengthening good governance.

a6484.speaker: Harold Aidoo, Executive Director of Integrity Watch-Liberia
a6484.speech: “Combined effort is needed to ensure that the ordinary people benefit from the natural resources in the country in the wake of USAID drawdown.”

a6608.speaker: Romania's Ministry of National Defence
a6608.speech: Said Romania scrambled fighter jets after a drone breached the country's airspace during a Russian attack on neighbouring Ukraine ; said it detected the drone incursion late on Saturday and scrambled two F-16 fighter jets as well as two Eurofighters – part of German air policing missions in Romania – while also warning citizens to take cover ; said the jets followed the drone until “it disappeared from the radar” near the Romanian village of Chilia Veche.

a6608.speaker: Ionut Mosteanu, Romanian Minister of National Defence
a6608.speech: Said the F-16 pilots came close to taking down the drone before it left the country's airspace, adding that helicopters would survey the area near the border to look for potential drone parts. “But all information at this moment indicates the drone exited airspace to Ukraine,” he told the private television station Antena 3.

a6608.speaker: Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President (post on X)
a6608.speech: Said data showed the drone breached about 10km (6 miles) into Romanian territory and operated in NATO airspace for about 50 minutes ; alleged that the Russian military knows exactly where its drones are headed and how long they can operate in the air ; “It is an obvious expansion of the war by Russia – and this is exactly how they act” ; “Sanctions against Russia are needed. Tariffs against Russian trade are needed. Collective defence is needed.”

a6608.speaker: Maria Malmer Stenergard, Swedish Minister for Foreign Affairs (post on X)
a6608.speech: Wrote that the breach was “another unacceptable violation of NATO airspace” ; “Sweden stands in full solidarity with Romania as a NATO Ally and EU Member State. We are always ready to contribute further to the deterrence and defence of the Alliance.”

a6608.speaker: NATO
a6608.speech: Had announced plans to beef up the defence of Europe's eastern flank on Friday, after Poland shot down drones that had violated its airspace.

a6608.speaker: Marco Rubio, United States Secretary of State
a6608.speech: Expressed concern at the Russian drone incursion into Polish airspace, but said that it remained unclear if it was a deliberate act by Russia. “We think it's an unacceptable and unfortunate and dangerous development,” Rubio told reporters before departing on a trip to Israel and the United Kingdom. “No doubt about it: the drones were intentionally launched. The question is whether the drones were targeted to go into Poland specifically” ; said that if the drones were targeted at Poland, “if the evidence leads us there, then obviously that'll be a highly escalatory move” ; “There are a number of other possibilities as well, but I think we'd like to have all the facts and consult with our allies before we make specific determinations.”

a6608.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a6608.speech: Suggested that the Russian incursions into Polish airspace were a mistake.

a6608.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (post on his Truth Social platform)
a6608.speech: Said on Saturday that he was ready to impose major sanctions on Russia – just as soon as all NATO nations did the same thing and stopped buying Russian oil: “I am ready to do major Sanctions on Russia when all NATO Nations have agreed, and started, to do the same thing, and when all NATO Nations STOP BUYING OIL FROM RUSSIA.”

a6608.speaker: Donald Tusk, Polish Prime Minister (post on X)
a6608.speech: Dismissed the suggestion that the incursion was a mistake: “We would also wish that the drone attack on Poland was a mistake. But it wasn't. And we know it.”

a6617.speaker: Monetary Policy Committee of the National Bank of Ethiopia (statement)
a6617.speech: Ironically, the statement from the Monetary Policy Committee sounded as if it were reporting on two different economies: on the surface, headline inflation cooled to 13.6pc in August, down from 18.8pc a year earlier; food prices eased, helped by a decent harvest; buoyant coffee and gold exports replenished reserves; and Treasury-bill yields slipped to 15pc in August from 17.6pc in June. Beneath that veneer, non-food inflation was stuck at 15.1pc, the Birr's weakness feeds into rents, transport and every imported good, liquidity pressures are biting at banks, and the policy rate, currently at 15pc, offers no relief to borrowers. ; For now, the Monetary Policy Committee's message appears plain: it prioritises price stability, and growth is secondary.

a6617.speaker: Bankers (unnamed)
a6617.speech: Eyob's decision produced cautious optimism, and a fair bit of scepticism, among bankers who have watched the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) tighten and loosen the taps for years without ever daring a wholesale overhaul; the Governor's latest move, they suspect, is another exercise in fine-tuning rather than a bold leap.

a6617.speaker: National Bank of Ethiopia (Central Bank data)
a6617.speech: Central Bank data from the fourth quarter of 2023/24 show commercial banks' liquidity ratio - actual reserves plus net foreign assets relative to demand deposits - was 13.8pc in June 2024; reserves on hand or parked with the Central Bank totalled 263.1 billion Br, while foreign assets were a further 143.9 billion Br. System-wide deposits reached 2.5 trillion Br in June 2024, up 15.3pc on the year, while outstanding credit, including corporate bonds, rose 10.1pc to 2.1 trillion Br, leaving the aggregate LDR at 60.5pc. ; Broad money grew by 23.1pc year-on-year, while base money expanded by a startling 70.7pc.

a6617.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a6617.speech: Pegs global growth at three percent for 2025.
